extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students, artists, and scholars interested in literary/arts techniques (pastiche, parody, homage)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for recognizing or producing pastiche across arts (literature, music, film, theatre, architecture). Emphasizes imitation of style, distinction from parody/allusion, and typical uses and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of style or character
rubrics_metrics.description: A pastiche is a work of visual art, literature, theatre, music, or architecture that imitates the style or character of the work of one or more other artists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core definitional criterion: the creator deliberately reproduces recognizable stylistic features of another artist or period. Applicable across media (writing, music, film, architecture, etc.). Examples on the page illustrate imitation of compositional, linguistic, cinematic, or architectural style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pays homage rather than mocks (distinct from parody)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike parody, pastiche pays homage to the work it imitates, rather than mocking it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing/evaluating a pastiche, assess whether the tone is celebratory/respectful rather than satirical or derisive. The page notes that style parodies can 'walk the line' between celebration (pastiche) and send-up (parody), so degree of mockery vs. tribute is a key axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not mere allusion — reiterates rather than merely references
rubrics_metrics.description: Allusion is not pastiche. A literary allusion may refer to another work, but it does not reiterate it. Allusion requires the audience to share in the author's cultural knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To qualify as pastiche, the work must actively reproduce or imitate stylistic elements rather than only include indirect references. Evaluate whether imitation/reiteration of style is present, not just mention or reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light‑hearted, tongue‑in‑cheek and usually respectful (literary usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary usage, the term denotes a literary technique employing a generally light‑hearted tongue‑in‑cheek imitation of another's style; although jocular, it is usually respectful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For literary pastiche, tone is important: playful and imitative rather than antagonistic. The page also notes the term's implication of lack of originality or coherence, though postmodern perspectives may view it positively as deliberate homage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative jumble / perceived lack of originality or coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: The word implies a lack of originality or coherence, an imitative jumble, but with the advent of postmodernism, pastiche has become positively construed as a deliberate, witty homage or playful imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a work as pastiche, consider whether it sacrifices unity/novelty in favor of stitched-together imitation; also consider whether that quality is intentional and artistically defended (postmodern positive reading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation/unauthorized continuations and character pastiches
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastiche may include posthumous continuations of stories or sequels written by other writers without authorization (e.g., continuations of Robert E. Howard's stories; Sherlock Holmes pastiches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fidelity to original author's voice/characters and whether the new piece purposefully mimics the source to extend or honour it. Legal/ethical status (authorization/blessing) is separate from being a pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical pastiche: imitation of earlier styles or combining distinct styles
rubrics_metrics.description: In music, pastiche can mean works in imitation of an earlier style (e.g., Mozart imitating Baroque; Grieg's Holberg Suite) or pieces that 'hodge‑podge' many distinct styles into one song (e.g., 'Bohemian Rhapsody').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess use of forms, harmonies, rhythms, instrumentation, and stylistic tropes of target periods/artists. Note the distinction between homage and plagiarism; 'style parodies' by artists like 'Weird Al' may approach parody rather than pure pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical theatre pastiche: evoke era via style and lyrics
rubrics_metrics.description: In musical theatre, pastiche is used to evoke the sounds of a particular era; composers/lyricists imitate not just musical patterns but also lyric styles (e.g., Sondheim writing songs in the style of 1920s–30s Broadway writers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate accuracy of period idioms (melody, harmony, rhythm) and lyric diction/structures; check whether the pastiche serves dramatic/evocative functions within the show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cinematic pastiche: imitate filmmaker's style and cinematic techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Pastiche can be a cinematic device whereby filmmakers pay homage to another filmmaker's style and use of cinematography, including camera angles, lighting, and mise en scène; writers may also imitate the writerly style of other films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating film pastiche, look for replicated visual grammar (framing, lighting, camera movement), thematic or plot elements, and narrative devices that signal the source filmmaker or era. Examples: Sergio Leone, Quentin Tarantino, Todd Haynes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural pastiche: imitation of historical building styles (often pejorative)
rubrics_metrics.description: In urban planning/architecture, 'pastiche' may describe developments as imitations of building styles created by major architects, with the implication that the derivative work is unoriginal and of little merit; the term is not always pejorative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess fidelity to historical motifs, materiality, and proportion, and consider whether the imitation serves contextual or aesthetic goals versus being merely derivative. The page cites both negative and neutral uses of the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastiche Mass: assembling movements from different Mass settings
rubrics_metrics.description: A pastiche Mass is a musical Mass where the constituent movements come from different Mass settings; performers may choose a Kyrie from one composer and a Gloria from another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a technical/performative criterion: evaluate coherence when disparate movements are combined, and whether the assembly is for concert practicality or artistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastiche as eclecticism or collaborative composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphorically, pastiche and pasticcio describe works that are either composed by several authors, or that incorporate stylistic elements of other artists' work. Pastiche is an example of eclecticism in art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing/evaluating such a work, examine how multiple authorship or mixed stylistic inputs are integrated and whether the composite achieves a coherent aesthetic or intentionally foregrounds heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary criterion: degree to which imitation becomes plagiarism or derivative work
rubrics_metrics.description: The article lists related concepts (derivative work, plagiarism, fair use) and implies a boundary between respectful homage (pastiche) and improper copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate legal/ethical considerations separately: degree of transformation, attribution/authorization, and originality are relevant when distinguishing acceptable pastiche from infringement or mere copying.
